items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Earl Warren, Buddy Tate and myself, we’re the only ones left of the Basie band.

ctx.x: It was just stock arrangements. We had two trumpets and a trombone and the other trumpet player, he used to play all the solos, play all the firsts and I was just sitting there. So, one night, we were playing at this Masonic Hall on Long Street and when his time came to play he was having a drink at the bar, so I took his solo. From then on, gee whiz, every time he’d get ready to take a solo, I’d say, “I got it.” That was my first solo on Limehouse Blues, I never will forget it. Gee whiz, that was a thrill to…

think very few people know this except the older guys, Earl Warren, Buddy Tate and myself, we’re the only ones left of the Basie band. They remember, but John Hammond, he was responsible for the Count Basie band, period, because he brought Basie to New York. They had, you remember, the Camel Hour, and all the bands used to do it. items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: So when Earl Warren would sing, "I struck a match in the dark," we were supposed to strike a match, you know, and light up the bandstand.

ctx.x: We were all sitting on the stage, you know. And we were sharp and everything. So when Earl Warren would sing, "I struck a match in the dark," we were supposed to strike a match, you know, and light up the bandstand. So when he said -- Earl Warren made the introduction, "I struck a match in the dark," Pres held up the arrangement and struck a match and burned up the whole arrangement. Burned his part up.
